title: Structure Prediction of Multi-Component Molecular Crystals with Genarris 4.0
summary: Multi-component molecular crystals are increasingly used in pharmaceuticals, organic electronics, and energetic materials because they can have unique, tunable properties that are not achievable in single-component crystals. Predicting the structure of multi-component crystals is more challenging, owing to the need to explore the larger space of multiple asymmetric unit configurations. We present a new version of the Genarris open-source molecular crystal structure generator, capable of treating multicomponent crystals. The main new feature of Genarris 4.0 is generation of asymmetric units (ASUs) from the input components and a workflow for selecting ASUs for crystal structure generation. For each ASU, crystal structures are generated in all space groups compatible with the requested number of ASUs per unit cell (Z). The Universal Model for Atoms (UMA) machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are used here for structure relaxation and energy evaluation within the workflow. Genarris 4.0 successfully predicts the structure of six targets: three co-crystals, two salts, and one crystal with Z ′ = 2. Because the UMA MLIPs were trained on single-component molecular crystals, we evaluate its performance for multi-component crystals by comparison to dispersion-inclusive density functional theory (DFT). We find that the results of relaxation and lattice energy ranking of putative structures obtained with UMA are in better agreement with DFT for co-crystals than for salts. Nevertheless, the UMA MLIPs perform well within the workflow, with all experimentally observed structures ranked first or second. Genarris 4.0 therefore provides an effective platform for multi-component crystal structure prediction and the generation of MLIPs training data.

screen.tldr: Genarris 4.0 extends molecular crystal structure prediction to multi-component crystals, using ASU generation and UMA MLIPs for relaxation and lattice-energy ranking.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Genarris 4.0, an open-source crystal structure generation workflow extended to multicomponent molecular crystals, and shows it can successfully predict several co-crystals, salts, and a Z' = 2 crystal using machine-learned potentials for relaxation and ranking.
AI.motivation: Multicomponent molecular crystals are important in pharmaceuticals, organic electronics, and energetic materials because they can exhibit tunable properties not available in single-component crystals. However, predicting their structures is harder due to the much larger configurational space of possible asymmetric-unit arrangements.
AI.method: The authors upgraded Genarris to generate asymmetric units (ASUs) from multiple input components and to select ASUs for structure generation. For each ASU, candidate crystal structures are generated across all space groups compatible with the target number of ASUs per unit cell (Z). The workflow uses the Universal Model for Atoms (UMA) machine-learned interatomic potentials for geometry relaxation and energy ranking, and benchmarks these results against dispersion-corrected DFT.
AI.result: Genarris 4.0 successfully predicted six test cases: three co-crystals, two salts, and one crystal with Z' = 2. UMA-based relaxations and rankings agreed better with DFT for co-crystals than for salts, likely reflecting the single-component training of the MLIPs. Even so, the experimentally observed structures were ranked first or second in all cases.
AI.conclusion: Genarris 4.0 is an effective platform for multicomponent crystal structure prediction. It can handle ASU generation and structure search for complex crystals, and the UMA MLIPs are sufficiently accurate for practical workflow use, while also being useful for generating training data for improved MLIPs.

title: Latent Genetic Algorithm for Crystal Structure Prediction
summary: Predicting crystal structures requires navigating rugged energy landscapes in which favorable local motifs must be inherited across candidates with incompatible cells, densities, and symmetries. Conventional real-space crossover often destroys these motifs when parent structures are geometrically mismatched. Here we show that latent representations learned by pretrained universal interatomic potentials can serve as continuous evolutionary coordinates for crystal structure prediction. In the Latent Genetic Algorithm (LGA), offspring are generated by inverse optimization of atomic positions and lattice vectors to match a target latent representation, which is constructed via interpolation of the parent latent vectors. LGA suppresses high-energy and short-contact offspring, increases the HfO$_2$ ground-state recovery rate from 20-35% to 60-95%, and enables a unified variable-supercell search over 16 perovskites with a nearly tenfold reduction in search cost. Applied to (PbTiO$_3$)$_n$/(PbZrO$_3$)$_n$ superlattices, LGA reveals $\sqrt{2} \times 3\sqrt{2} \times 1$ long-period ground-state structures characterized by a common in-plane finite-$q$ modulation $q{_\parallel} = (1/6,1/6)$ and layer-coupled sidebands. To our knowledge, this in-plane periodicity has not been reported in any related oxide perovskite superlattice studies. Altogether, LGA offers a powerful representation-guided paradigm for ground-state structure prediction and provides a practical, decoder-free route toward materials inverse design.

screen.tldr: Latent Genetic Algorithm uses pretrained universal interatomic potential embeddings to guide crystal structure search, boosting recovery and finding long-period perovskite superlattice ground states.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Latent Genetic Algorithm (LGA) that uses pretrained interatomic-potential latent spaces as evolutionary coordinates to generate crystal-structure offspring, improving structure prediction robustness and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Conventional real-space crossover often fails for crystal structure prediction because parent structures may differ in cell shape, density, and symmetry, which destroys useful local motifs and leads to poor offspring quality.
AI.method: LGA performs inverse optimization of atomic positions and lattice vectors so the generated structure matches an interpolated target latent representation derived from parent latent vectors. This latent-space guidance is used for variable-supercell crystal searches.
AI.result: The method reduces high-energy and short-contact offspring, raises HfO2 ground-state recovery from 20–35% to 60–95%, and achieves nearly a tenfold search-cost reduction across 16 perovskites. For (PbTiO3)n/(PbZrO3)n superlattices, it identifies long-period ground states with a sqrt(2) x 3sqrt(2) x 1 periodicity and an in-plane finite-q modulation q_parallel = (1/6,1/6).
AI.conclusion: Latent representations from pretrained universal interatomic potentials can act as effective continuous coordinates for crystal evolution, enabling a decoder-free and more reliable paradigm for ground-state structure prediction and materials inverse design.

title: A Distributional Framework for Generative Modeling of Molecular Crystals
summary: Molecular crystals are a highly polymorphic class of materials, with a single molecule commonly crystallizing via multiple packing patterns, making structure and property prediction very challenging. Crystal structure prediction typically comprises the production of sets of promising candidate structures, each considered in isolation rather than as samples in a thermodynamic distribution. Likewise, modern generative approaches to this problem, despite naturally sampling distributions of crystals, lack a concrete formulation of the distributions being sampled. Two components are required to impart meaning to the distributions of crystals generated under such models: a canonical parameterization, and a loss function which equilibrates the generated samples to some target distribution. We develop such a parameterization, and train energy-based generative flow networks (GFlowNets) to approximate the Boltzmann distribution over crystal structures for target molecules and space groups. Combined, these components comprise our MXtalGFlow framework for molecular crystal modeling. Going beyond sampling disconnected sets of low-energy structures, MXtalGFlow yields a thermodynamic distribution over crystal structures. We sample and analyze distributions of crystals for two molecules, each under two energy functions, a Lennard-Jones potential and the Universal Model for Atoms. We characterize the local structural basins about the known polymorphs, and identify additional as-yet un-reported packing modes with competitive probabilities to the known experimental structures. With MXtalGFlow, we illustrate how to define and train a model to sample a thermodynamically meaningful distribution of molecular crystals, and analyze such a distribution to glean useful information.

screen.tldr: Introduces MXtalGFlow, a distributional generative framework that samples Boltzmann-like ensembles of molecular crystal structures and analyzes polymorph basins.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MXtalGFlow, a framework that models molecular crystal structures as a thermodynamic distribution rather than as isolated candidate predictions, using a canonical crystal parameterization and energy-based GFlowNets to approximate Boltzmann distributions.
AI.motivation: Crystal structure prediction is difficult because one molecule can form many polymorphs, and existing methods usually return disconnected low-energy candidates without a principled probabilistic interpretation. The authors aim to make generated crystal samples thermodynamically meaningful.
AI.method: They develop a canonical parameterization for molecular crystals and train energy-based generative flow networks (GFlowNets) to sample crystal structures according to a target Boltzmann distribution for given molecules and space groups. They evaluate the framework on two molecules under two energy models: Lennard-Jones and the Universal Model for Atoms.
AI.result: MXtalGFlow produces distributions over crystal structures rather than isolated structures, and the sampled distributions reveal local basins around known polymorphs as well as additional previously unreported packing modes with probabilities comparable to experimental structures.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that molecular crystal generation can be formulated as learning a thermodynamically meaningful distribution, and that this approach can provide both better sampling and deeper insight into polymorphism and competing crystal packings.

title: Fully Atomistic Vibrational Free Energy of Molecular Crystals Using Distributed Multipole Moments
summary: Predicting the most stable crystal structure of a given molecule remains a longstanding challenge. Crystal structure prediction (CSP) is the computational area of research seeking to identify all stable and metastable structures of a given compound using solely the two dimensional molecular connectivity diagram as input. The reliable stability ranking of hypothetical crystal structures at finite temperature requires the evaluation of the Gibbs free energies of a myriad computer-generated crystal structures. Current CSP workflows mostly rely on static (0 K) lattice energy differences due to the difficulties and computational cost associated with calculating entropic and other temperature-dependent free energy contributions. In some cases, a small number of structures are assessed via vibrational free energy calculation methods that either employ computationally demanding atomistic electronic structure calculations or force field approaches under the rigid-body approximation. There is a need to develop methods that offer a better compromise between accuracy and computational cost. In this work, we derive, for the first time, lattice dynamics expressions that allow for a fully atomistic treatment of molecular flexibility with a commonly used force field in CSP, relying on distributed multipole moments for the description of electrostatic interactions. We implement these expressions in the CrystalDynamics algorithm to calculate dispersion curves, phonon density of states and vibrational free energies and we demonstrate its application to molecular crystals of three compounds of increasing size and molecular flexibility. The analytical derivations underlying our proposed methodology result in an efficient and robust evaluation of the free energy of molecular crystals. Our work facilitates the study of relative stability as a function of temperature, enabling the evaluation of enantiotropic transitions between crystal forms. Thanks to its low computational cost our suggested method can be integrated into CSP protocols to bridge the gap between static lattice energies computed at 0 K and temperature-dependent free energies.

screen.tldr: Derives and implements fully atomistic lattice-dynamics free-energy calculations for molecular crystals, enabling finite-temperature polymorph ranking beyond rigid-body approximations.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a low-cost lattice-dynamics method for crystal structure prediction that computes temperature-dependent vibrational free energies with full molecular flexibility using a force field and distributed multipoles, improving stability ranking beyond 0 K lattice energies.
AI.motivation: Current crystal structure prediction workflows usually rely on static lattice energies at 0 K because accurate free-energy calculations are expensive. Existing vibrational approaches are often either too costly or limited by rigid-body approximations, creating a need for a method that balances accuracy and computational efficiency.
AI.method: The authors derive analytical lattice-dynamics expressions for a fully atomistic treatment of flexible molecular crystals using a common force field and distributed multipole electrostatics. They implement these expressions in the CrystalDynamics algorithm to compute dispersion curves, phonon density of states, and vibrational free energies, and test the approach on three molecular crystals of increasing size and flexibility.
AI.result: The method enables efficient and robust free-energy evaluation for molecular crystals and can assess temperature-dependent relative stability, including enantiotropic transitions between crystal forms. It is demonstrated to be computationally inexpensive enough for integration into CSP workflows.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a practical bridge between static 0 K lattice-energy ranking and finite-temperature free-energy ranking in crystal structure prediction, offering a more scalable route to predicting stable crystal forms.

title: Best practices in `0 K' DFT energy calculations on molecular crystal structures
comment: Acta Crystallographica Section C Structural Chemistry
summary: This article describes best practices for `zero Kelvin' energy calculations on molecular crystals and is targeted for non-experts who would like to perform their own calculations or assess the accuracy and validity of such calculations reported in the scientific literature. The recommended computational procedure can be summarized as follows. (1) Energy optimize the crystal structures of interest with a suitable dispersion-corrected density functional, such as PBE (abbreviated here as PBE+D). (2) Based on the extent of geometric distortions after energy minimization, decide if subsequent energy calculations are required and meaningful. (3) Decide if the PBE+D crystal energies suffice; if they do not, perform a single-point energy calculation on the molecular crystal with a hybrid exchange-correlation functional, such as PBE0, again with a suitable dispersion correction. Similarly, decide if single-point energy calculations on the individual molecules with a more accurate level of theory, such as MP2D or ωB97X+D, are required to improve the molecular energies to account for multiple conformations or tautomers.
raw_categories: Acta Crystallographica Section C Structural Chemistry

screen.tldr: Practical guidance for zero-K DFT energy ranking of molecular crystal structures, including dispersion-corrected optimization and higher-level single-point corrections.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a practical workflow for reliable zero-Kelvin energy calculations of molecular crystals, combining dispersion-corrected DFT geometry optimization with selective higher-level single-point energy refinements.
AI.motivation: It aims to help non-experts perform their own calculations and evaluate the reliability of reported crystal energy results in the literature.
AI.method: First, optimize crystal structures using a dispersion-corrected density functional such as PBE+D. Then assess whether the geometry changes are small enough to justify further calculations. If needed, compute crystal single-point energies with a higher-level hybrid functional such as PBE0 plus dispersion correction. For molecular reference energies, optionally refine individual molecule energies using more accurate methods such as MP2D or ωB97X+D, especially when multiple conformations or tautomers matter.
AI.result: The article provides a stepwise best-practice protocol for deciding when simple PBE+D results are sufficient and when more accurate single-point calculations are warranted for both crystals and isolated molecules.
AI.conclusion: Reliable zero-Kelvin molecular crystal energetics require a balance between computational cost and accuracy, with geometry optimization at dispersion-corrected DFT as the baseline and higher-level single-point corrections applied only when necessary.

title: Engineering Small-Molecule Proton-Transfer Ferroelectrics by Crystal Structure Prediction: Design Limits at the Salt–Cocrystal Boundary
summary: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Organic molecular ferroelectrics hold significant potential in organic electronics due to their chemical tunability and straightforward fabrication methods. Among these, acid–base proton-transfer (PT) salts are notable for their low coercive fields and fast switching capabilities but are limited by relatively low spontaneous polarization. Using smaller molecular species can in principle increase the polarization, but requires both stabilization of the monovalent salt state and crystal packing that supports ferroelectric PT pathways. Using a crystal-structure prediction (CSP)-based design combined with density functional theory (DFT), we investigate 30 combinations of molecular acids and bases aimed at enhancing the dipole density. We identified several crystal structures with PT-capable hydrogen-bonding networks, and in our initial DFT ranking, three candidate ferroelectric packings and one antiferroelectric. Subsequent experimental work on two representative systems, while confirming the ability of CSP to predict PT-capable packing motifs, found neutral cocrystals rather than the desired monovalent salts supporting ferroelectricity. More detailed computational analysis traced the disparity to the relative stability of protonation states, which is strongly sensitive to the exchange–correlation functional and to vibrational zero-point energy contributions. Thus, while our CSP study correctly identified proton-transfer crystal packing motifs, it failed at the level of protonation-state stability, which we found to be strongly influenced by exchange–correlation choice and vibrational free energy.

screen.tldr: CSP and DFT are used to design small-molecule proton-transfer ferroelectrics, revealing PT-capable packings but also functional-sensitive salt–cocrystal stability limits.

AI.tldr: The study uses crystal-structure prediction and DFT to search for small-molecule proton-transfer ferroelectrics with higher polarization, but experiments show neutral cocrystals instead of the targeted monovalent salts. The work demonstrates that packing motifs can be predicted well, while protonation-state stability is much harder to predict and depends strongly on the functional and vibrational effects.
AI.motivation: Organic molecular ferroelectrics are attractive for organic electronics because they are chemically tunable and easy to process. Proton-transfer salts are especially promising due to low coercive fields and fast switching, but their spontaneous polarization is often too low. The authors aim to increase dipole density by using smaller molecular species while maintaining stable proton-transfer ferroelectric behavior.
AI.method: The authors combined crystal-structure prediction (CSP) with density functional theory (DFT) to screen 30 acid-base pairs for ferroelectric proton-transfer candidates. They ranked predicted structures by their ferroelectric or antiferroelectric character, then performed experiments on two representative systems. They also carried out additional computational analysis to examine protonation-state stability, including the effects of exchange-correlation functional choice and vibrational zero-point energy.
AI.result: CSP identified several crystal structures with hydrogen-bond networks suitable for proton transfer, including three candidate ferroelectric packings and one antiferroelectric in the initial DFT ranking. Experiments confirmed that CSP could predict the relevant packing motifs, but the actual products were neutral cocrystals rather than the intended monovalent salts. Further analysis showed that the mismatch arose from incorrect prediction of protonation-state stability, which is highly sensitive to the DFT functional and vibrational contributions.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that CSP is effective for finding proton-transfer-capable crystal packings, but not sufficient on its own to predict whether the desired protonated salt state will be thermodynamically stable. Accurate design of organic ferroelectrics therefore requires improved treatment of protonation energetics, especially exchange-correlation effects and vibrational free energy.

title: Interfacial Nucleation Pathways Governing Polymorph Selection Revealed by Synchrotron-Based In Situ GIWAXS and Molecular Simulations
comment: Journal of the American Chemical Society
summary: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Gas–liquid interfacial nucleation can influence organic crystallization, yet its mechanistic role in polymorph selection remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that nucleation at the gas–liquid interface of flufenamic acid solutions governs polymorph selection and gives rise to a pronounced concentration-dependent polymorphism, wherein low initial concentrations favor the nucleation of form I, higher concentrations yield form III, and intermediate concentrations selectively produce the metastable form IV. In situ synchrotron-based grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) directly resolves the formation and evolution of prenucleation assemblies at the interface, revealing three distinct interfacial molecular evolution pathways correlated with the emergence of specific polymorphs. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with energy calculations within the hybrid quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) embedded-cluster framework further reveal interfacial enrichment, orientational bias, and conformer-dependent stabilization of stacking motifs, providing a microscopic interpretation of the experimentally observed selectivity. Together, these results establish the gas–liquid interface as an active structural selector that reshapes molecular organization prior to nucleation, offering a mechanistic framework for understanding and controlling polymorphism in evaporation-driven crystallization.

AI.motivation: Polymorph selection in organic crystallization is still poorly understood, especially how interfacial nucleation at the gasliquid boundary affects which crystal form appears. The work aims to clarify the microscopic mechanism behind concentration-dependent polymorphism.
AI.method: The authors combined in situ synchrotron grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) to track interfacial prenucleation assemblies with molecular dynamics simulations and hybrid QM/MM embedded-cluster energy calculations to analyze molecular enrichment, orientation, conformational effects, and stacking stabilization at the interface.

AI.conclusion: The gasliquid interface is not a passive boundary but an active structural selector that reorganizes molecules before nucleation and thereby determines polymorph outcome. This provides a mechanistic basis for controlling polymorphism in evaporation-driven crystallization.

title: Structure and Stability Prediction of Binary and Ternary Molecular Mixed Crystals Using Ensemble Free Energies
summary: Mixed crystals provide a route to tune the properties of molecular solids through continuous changes in composition. However, predicting their stability is challenging because it requires determining both substitution energies and configurational entropy across large configuration spaces. Here, we combine crystal structure prediction, force field lattice energy calculations, and ∆-machine-learning energy corrections with a scaled partition-function approach to assess structure prediction and evaluate binary and ternary mixed crystals of anthracene (ANT), acridine (ACR), and phenazine (PNZ). The composition-dependent ensemble free energy (∆G ensemble ) was estimated without exhaustive enumeration of all configurations from representative ensembles of substituted supercell models of mixed crystals. Crystal structure prediction reproduces the known polymorphs as the lowest energy structures and the mixed crystal modelling approach reproduces the main experimental binary trends: ACR incorporation into ANT and the α and β polymorphs of PNZ, ANT incorporation into ACR form II, and the formation of a PNZ β-type phase. Furthermore, we predict additional thermodynamically stable compositions, including PNZ incorporation into ACR form IX, and ternary crystals based on ACR forms II, VI and VII. Stable three-component regions arise from binary trends, with ACR mediating between both ANT and PNZ. These results demonstrate a practical framework for predicting the structure, thermodynamic stability and composition limits of molecular mixed crystals.

screen.tldr: Uses CSP, force-field lattice energies, and Δ-machine-learning corrections to predict structures and ensemble free energies of binary and ternary molecular mixed crystals.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a practical computational framework for predicting the structures and thermodynamic stability of binary and ternary molecular mixed crystals, using anthracene, acridine, and phenazine as a case study.
AI.motivation: Mixed crystals can tune molecular-solid properties through composition, but their stability is hard to predict because one must account for substitution energetics and configurational entropy over many possible arrangements.
AI.method: The authors combine crystal structure prediction, force-field lattice energy calculations, delta-machine-learning corrections, and a scaled partition-function approach. They estimate composition-dependent ensemble free energies from representative substituted supercell ensembles rather than exhaustively enumerating all configurations.
AI.result: The approach reproduces known polymorphs as the lowest-energy structures and matches key experimental binary behaviors, including ACR in ANT and PNZ, ANT in ACR form II, and a PNZ beta-type phase. It also predicts additional stable compositions, such as PNZ in ACR form IX and ternary crystals based on ACR forms II, VI, and VII.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that combining structure prediction with efficient free-energy estimation can successfully identify stable mixed-crystal compositions and phase limits, offering a useful route for designing molecular mixed crystals.

title: Epimer-Dependent Solid-State Landscapes of Trospium and Exotrospium Halide Salts
summary: Trospium (TR) and exotrospium (ETR) form a closely related epimeric pair of quaternary ammonium compounds, differing only in the stereochemistry of the tropane ring system. While the solid-state chemistry of trospium has been studied mainly for its chloride salt, no crystal structures of exotrospium salts have previously been reported. Here, we investigate the epimerdependent solid-state landscapes of TR and ETR across the halide series, using matched salt forms to distinguish the effects of counterion selection from those of stereochemical inversion. Two new TR salts and three new ETR salts were prepared and structurally characterized by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, supported by crystal-packing comparison, hydrogen-bond propensity analysis, lattice-energy calculations, morphology prediction, and CSD-Particle surface analysis. Despite their close molecular similarity, TR and ETR display markedly different solid-state behaviour. TR forms anhydrous chloride, bromide, and iodide salts stabilized by direct charge-assisted OH···halide interactions, whereas ETR forms isostructural chloride and bromide dihydrates, with only the iodide obtained as an anhydrate. These differences are reflected in molecular conformation, crystal packing, hydration behaviour, predicted crystal habit, and surface descriptors. The results show that epimerization can substantially alter both bulk and surface features of pharmaceutical molecular salts and demonstrate the value of combining structural comparison with particle-level descriptors when evaluating related solid forms.

AI.motivation: The authors aimed to understand how epimerization affects the solid-state behavior of closely related pharmaceutical salts, especially because exotrospium salt crystal structures had not been reported and trospium had been studied mainly as the chloride salt.
AI.method: Matched halide salts of TR and ETR were prepared and characterized by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. The study also used crystal-packing comparison, hydrogen-bond propensity analysis, lattice-energy calculations, morphology prediction, and CSD-Particle surface analysis to compare solid-state and surface-level properties.
AI.result: Two new TR salts and three new ETR salts were obtained. TR formed anhydrous chloride, bromide, and iodide salts stabilized by direct charge-assisted OH···halide interactions. In contrast, ETR formed isostructural chloride and bromide dihydrates, while only the iodide was anhydrous. The two epimers differed in molecular conformation, packing, hydration tendency, predicted crystal habit, and surface descriptors.
AI.conclusion: Epimerization can strongly reshape both bulk and surface properties of pharmaceutical salts, even when the molecules are very similar. The work highlights the importance of combining structural analysis with particle-level descriptors when evaluating related solid forms.

title: Adaptive fine-tuning of foundation models for crystal structure prediction: Discovery of high-pressure phases in the CaFeNi system
summary: The prediction of crystal structures is a key challenge in chemistry and materials science, but evolutionary crystal structure prediction (CSP) remains computationally expensive because it relies on repeated \textit{ab initio} relaxations and energy ranking. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can accelerate CSP, yet their use is limited by the need for large training sets and by the difficulty of choosing which candidate structures should be labeled by density functional theory (DFT). Here we introduce a self-consistent, foundation-model-assisted CSP workflow that combines evolutionary search with adaptive data selection and fine-tuning. Starting from a pretrained MLIP, the algorithm rapidly explores configuration space while iteratively selecting compact, representative, and physically relevant subsets of structures for DFT labeling, thereby reducing redundant calculations and improving a system-specific potential. We apply the method to the chemically complex Ca--Fe--Ni ternary system. The workflow reproduces the known low-pressure convex hull and enables efficient high-pressure exploration. It predicts a previously unreported compound, Ca$_6$FeNi, which becomes thermodynamically stable above 100~GPa. These results show that foundation-model-based, data-efficient CSP can greatly reduce computational cost while preserving accuracy and enabling the discovery of new materials in complex multicomponent systems.

AI.motivation: Evolutionary crystal structure prediction is accurate but expensive because it requires many ab initio relaxations and energy evaluations. Existing MLIP-based acceleration is limited by large training data requirements and by uncertainty over which candidate structures should be labeled with DFT.
AI.method: The authors propose a self-consistent CSP workflow that starts from a pretrained foundation-model MLIP, performs evolutionary exploration of configuration space, and iteratively selects compact, representative, and physically relevant structure subsets for DFT labeling. The labeled data are used to fine-tune the potential during the search.

title: Evaluating Global Optimization and Generative Methods for Low-Energy and Diverse Crystal Structure Prediction Via Two Case Studies
summary: Accurate crystal structure prediction (CSP) is essential for discovering novel materials. Although various CSP methods have been developed, systematic benchmarks and quantitative comparisons remain limited. In this study, we evaluate eight CSP approaches: the evolutionary algorithm USPEX, three versions of ab initio random sampling with symmetry constraints (USPEX, AIRSS, Pyxtal codes), generative machine learning models (generative adversarial neural network, GAN, and variational autoencoder, VAE), and two very different template-based structure generators (random topological structure generator of USPEX and CSPML). These tests are done through a case study on vanadium oxide systems V5O8 and V3O4. Our results show that most of the compared methods are capable of identifying low-energy and metastable structures when sufficient sampling is performed. However, each method exhibits distinct strengths and trade-offs in terms of accuracy, efficiency, structural diversity, and symmetry character. Notably, more established traditional methods, such as USPEX and AIRSS, offer robust performance across system sizes, while ML-based approaches demonstrate rapid structure generation with minimal sampling, albeit with a greater reliance on the quality of the training data and post-processing approaches. Interestingly, different versions of random sampling show very different performance. This study underscores the complementary nature of traditional and ML-based CSP strategies and provides practical guidance for selecting appropriate methods based on the complexity of the system, the computational resources available, and the specific discovery objectives.

screen.tldr: Benchmark compares USPEX, AIRSS, PyXtal, GAN, VAE, and template-based generators for low-energy crystal prediction on two vanadium oxide case studies.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks eight crystal structure prediction (CSP) methods on vanadium oxide systems and finds that both traditional and machine-learning approaches can recover low-energy structures, but with different trade-offs in robustness, speed, diversity, and dependence on training data.
AI.motivation: Systematic benchmarks and quantitative comparisons of CSP methods are still limited, despite the importance of CSP for discovering new materials. The study aims to clarify how different CSP strategies perform in practice and when each is most suitable.
AI.method: A case-study benchmark was performed on two vanadium oxide systems, V5O8 and V3O4. Eight CSP approaches were compared: evolutionary search (USPEX), three symmetry-constrained ab initio random sampling implementations (USPEX, AIRSS, Pyxtal), two generative ML models (GAN and VAE), and two template-based generators (USPEX random topological generator and CSPML). Performance was assessed in terms of ability to find low-energy/metastable structures, efficiency, structural diversity, and symmetry characteristics.
AI.result: Most methods could identify low-energy and metastable structures given sufficient sampling. Traditional methods such as USPEX and AIRSS were generally robust across system sizes. ML-based methods generated structures quickly with minimal sampling, but their performance depended more strongly on training data quality and post-processing. The different random-sampling implementations showed notably different behavior, indicating that implementation details matter substantially.
AI.conclusion: CSP methods are complementary rather than universally superior. Traditional approaches are more robust and broadly reliable, while ML-based approaches offer speed and efficient generation but require careful training and refinement. The study provides practical guidance for choosing CSP methods based on system complexity, available computational resources, and discovery goals.

title: Interaction Hierarchy and Polymorphic Structure–Property Dynamics in Luminescent Molecular Crystals
summary: Solid-state phase transitions provide a powerful platform for translating subtle molecular-level interactions into macroscopic functional responses; however, rational design strategies that enable predictable control over such transitions remain limited. Herein, we report polymorphic structure-property switching behaviors associated with competing intermolecular interactions in luminescent molecular crystals. Cyano-β-substituted distyrylbenzene derivatives bearing bromo and methoxy side chains were designed to incorporate competing homotypic and heterotypic noncovalent interactions with distinct interaction characteristics. Single-crystal analyses reveal that subtle differences in the hierarchical ordering of dispersion-, dipole-dipole-, and electrostatically dominated interactions give rise to polymorphic crystal structures with distinct molecular orientations and photoluminescence properties. Thermal and mechanical stimuli induce distinct phase transitions: an irreversible thermally induced single-crystal-to-single-crystal transition and a pseudo-reversible mechanochemical pathway via an amorphous intermediate, both directly visualized as pronounced emission color changes. Kinetic and thermodynamic controls over polymorph formation are elucidated through a combination of structural analysis, photophysical measurements, and crystal framework calculations. This study suggests that multifunctional molecular side chains enable access to diverse interaction landscapes, allowing multiple structure-property switching pathways to be encoded within a single molecular framework. The presented framework provides a qualitative perspective for interpreting dynamic structural behaviors in molecular crystals.

screen.tldr: Luminescent molecular crystals show polymorph-dependent phase transitions driven by competing noncovalent interactions, with structure-property switching mapped by crystal analyses and framework calculations.
screen.transfer_note: Interaction hierarchy and polymorph-dependent transitions could inform ranking of competing crystal packings and finite-temperature stability in CSP workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that carefully designed side chains in luminescent molecular crystals can encode competing intermolecular interactions, enabling controllable polymorphism and stimulus-responsive emission switching.
AI.motivation: The work addresses the limited ability to rationally predict and control solid-state phase transitions by linking subtle molecular interactions to macroscopic optical responses.
AI.method: Cyano-β-substituted distyrylbenzene derivatives with bromo and methoxy side chains were synthesized and studied using single-crystal structure analysis, photoluminescence measurements, thermal and mechanical stimulus tests, and crystal framework calculations to compare interaction hierarchies and phase behavior.
AI.result: The compounds formed polymorphs with distinct molecular orientations and emission properties due to differences in dispersion-, dipole-dipole-, and electrostatic interactions. Thermal stimulation produced an irreversible single-crystal-to-single-crystal transition, while mechanical stimulation followed a pseudo-reversible pathway through an amorphous intermediate, both accompanied by visible emission color changes.
AI.conclusion: Multifunctional side chains can create multiple interaction landscapes within one molecular scaffold, enabling diverse and programmable structure-property switching pathways. The study provides a qualitative framework for understanding and designing dynamic behaviors in molecular crystals.

title: Resolution of chiral drug cocrystals: complementary roles of NMR, low-frequency Raman and vibrational circular dichroism
summary: Reliable discrimination of diastereomeric pharmaceutical cocrystals remains a significant analytical challenge, particularly when structural differences are subtle or when monocrystals suitable for X-ray diffraction are not available or difficult to prepare. Here, we compare the performance of four spectroscopic techniques, solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (ssNMR), Raman spectroscopy, infrared (IR) absorption, and solid-state vibrational circular dichroism (ssVCD), in terms of the resolution of model diastereomeric cocrystals. The first pair of diastereomeric cocrystals, (S)-naproxen with (R)- and (S)-alanine, represents an example of systems with pronounced packing differences, whereas the cocrystals of (R)-ivabradine hydrochloride with (R)- and (S)-mandelic acid are nearly isostructural diastereomers. The NMR and vibrational spectra were interpreted based on density functional theory (DFT) simulations, allowing for a detailed spectra-structure assignment and analysis. Although all techniques detected cocrystal formation, their practical discriminatory power toward diastereomers varied. VCD spectroscopy provided reliable differentiation, even for nearly isostructural systems, although the data were hampered by the experimental noise. Raman spectroscopy, especially in the low-frequency region, was effective for a rapid detection of distinct packing motifs but less sensitive for the closely related structures. ssNMR provides a complementary localized insight. The results indicate the advantages and drawbacks of using Raman spectroscopy, ssNMR, and VCD for screening, structural studies, and chiral identification of pharmaceutical cocrystals and other chiral complex solid-state systems.

screen.tldr: Compares ssNMR, Raman, IR, and VCD for distinguishing diastereomeric pharmaceutical cocrystals, using DFT-backed spectral assignments to resolve subtle packing differences.
screen.transfer_note: Low-frequency Raman and DFT-assisted spectral assignment could help validate and discriminate closely related cocrystal or polymorph candidates in CSP workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper compares ssNMR, Raman, IR, and ssVCD for distinguishing diastereomeric pharmaceutical cocrystals, finding that ssVCD is the most reliable for subtle cases, Raman is useful for rapid screening of packing differences, and ssNMR offers complementary local structural information.
AI.motivation: Reliable identification of diastereomeric cocrystals is difficult when structural differences are small and single-crystal X-ray diffraction is unavailable, so the study aims to evaluate which spectroscopic methods best discriminate such systems.
AI.method: Two model diastereomeric cocrystal pairs were examined: (S)-naproxen with (R)-/ (S)-alanine and (R)-ivabradine hydrochloride with (R)-/ (S)-mandelic acid. The authors compared ssNMR, Raman, IR, and ssVCD, and used DFT simulations to interpret and assign the observed spectra.
AI.result: All methods confirmed cocrystal formation, but their ability to distinguish diastereomers differed. ssVCD gave the most reliable discrimination, including for nearly isostructural cocrystals, though experimental noise limited data quality. Raman spectroscopy, especially in the low-frequency region, detected different packing motifs well but was less effective for very similar structures. ssNMR provided localized, complementary structural insight.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that no single technique is universally sufficient, but ssVCD is strongest for subtle chiral discrimination, Raman is valuable for fast screening of packing differences, and ssNMR is useful as a complementary structural probe for pharmaceutical cocrystals and related chiral solid-state systems.

title: Solvation‐Driven Modulation of Crystal Packing in Metacetamol: Insights From X‐Ray Diffraction, Hirshfeld, and Void Analyses
summary: ABSTRACT The crystal structures of metacetamol form I, hemihydrate, and acetone hemisolvate were investigated using single‐crystal x‐ray diffraction, complemented by Hirshfeld surface, fingerprint, energy framework, and void analyses. Comparative evaluation reveals that structural differences among these forms primarily stem from variations in hydrogen‐bonding networks and packing efficiency. Form I exhibits the most compact arrangement, stabilized by O–H···O and N–H···O hydrogen bonds in conjunction with π–π stacking, resulting in a dense and efficient packing motif. In contrast, the hemihydrate highlights the role of lattice water, which establishes an extended hydrogen‐bonding framework that disrupts aromatic stacking and enlarges void volume, thereby reducing packing density. The acetone hemisolvate displays the most fragmented and voluminous voids, stabilized predominantly by N–H···O = C and O–H···O = C interactions with solvent molecules. Fingerprint plots confirm the prevalence of H···H contacts, with notable contributions from O···H/H···O interactions. Quantitative void analysis demonstrates a progressive decline in packing efficiency across the series: form I (10.194%) < hemihydrate (12.793%) < acetone hemisolvate (12.983%). Energy framework analysis indicates variations in electrostatic and dispersion interaction contributions across the crystal forms, reflecting differences in intermolecular interaction networks. These results underscore the impact of solvation on intermolecular interactions and crystal packing, offering valuable insights for pharmaceutical solid‐state design.

screen.tldr: Compares metacetamol polymorph, hydrate, and solvated crystal packings using diffraction, Hirshfeld surfaces, energy frameworks, and void analysis to explain solvation effects.
screen.transfer_note: Energy-framework and void analyses could help rank candidate polymorphs and solvates by packing efficiency and intermolecular interaction patterns.

AI.tldr: The study compares three crystal forms of metacetamol and shows that solvation changes hydrogen-bonding patterns, packing efficiency, void space, and interaction energies, with the unsolvated form packing most efficiently and the solvates being less compact.
AI.motivation: The work aims to understand how different solid forms of a pharmaceutical compound differ in crystal packing and intermolecular interactions, which is important for solid-state design and formulation.
AI.method: Single-crystal X-ray diffraction was used to determine the structures, supported by Hirshfeld surface analysis, fingerprint plots, energy framework analysis, and void analysis to quantify contacts, interaction energies, and packing efficiency.
AI.result: Form I forms the densest packing through O–H···O, N–H···O hydrogen bonds and π–π stacking. The hemihydrate introduces lattice water that builds an extended hydrogen-bond network, disrupts aromatic stacking, and increases void volume. The acetone hemisolvate shows the most fragmented packing and largest voids, dominated by solvent-mediated hydrogen bonds. Void analysis indicates packing efficiency decreases from form I to hemihydrate to acetone hemisolvate, and fingerprint plots show H···H contacts are most common with significant O···H/H···O contributions.
AI.conclusion: Solvation substantially alters intermolecular interactions and crystal packing in metacetamol, reducing packing efficiency and increasing void space. The combined structural and energetic analyses provide useful guidance for pharmaceutical crystal engineering and solid-state optimization.

title: An influence of intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonding on crystal structure stability and density: dance of amino and nitro groups around the pyrazole ring
summary: Hydrogen bond plays an important role in chemistry and chemical technology. Plenty of works are related to investigation of weak, moderate and strong hydrogen bonds and their influence on the structure and properties. In this work two pairs of isomers of dinitro-N-aminopyrazole and dinitro-diaminopyrazole which were synthesized and characterized earlier are considered as model compounds to study both intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonding. The choice of isomers is related to the fact that having the same composition, such isomeric molecules differ in structure, and this difference and its influence on the crystal packing can be directly investigated. Using Δ OED densification approach, the role of each molecular unit (NH 2 and NO 2 groups and pyrazole ring) in a molecule itself and in crystal structure was investigated. This allowed us to conclude that while intermolecular hydrogen bonding is merely one type of intermolecular interaction among others, it is the intramolecular H-bond between amino and nitro groups that is the key interaction which allows molecules to actively participate in intermolecular bonding that, in turn, leads to close crystal packing thereby increasing crystal density, melting point and detonation properties.

screen.tldr: Compares isomeric nitro/aminopyrazoles to dissect how intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonding affect crystal packing, density, and stability in energetic molecular crystals.
screen.transfer_note: Highlights how intramolecular conformational preferences shape packing motifs and density, useful for ranking flexible-molecule crystal candidates.

AI.tldr: The paper studies two pairs of isomeric dinitro pyrazole derivatives to compare intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonding and its effect on crystal packing and material properties.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to understand how hydrogen bonding influences molecular structure, crystal organization, and resulting physical properties, especially by comparing isomers with the same composition but different connectivity.
AI.method: They analyze previously synthesized and characterized isomers using the ΔOED densification approach to quantify the contribution of molecular fragments such as NH2, NO2, and the pyrazole ring to both isolated molecules and crystal structures.
AI.result: The analysis indicates that intermolecular hydrogen bonding is only one of several packing interactions, whereas the intramolecular H-bond between amino and nitro groups is the key factor enabling stronger intermolecular bonding, tighter crystal packing, higher density, higher melting point, and improved detonation-related properties.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that intramolecular hydrogen bonding can indirectly control macroscopic crystal properties by promoting favorable intermolecular interactions and denser packing in isomeric nitro-pyrazole compounds.

title: Piezoelectricityfrom Dopant-Induced Structural Distortionsin Molecular Crystals Revealed by Raman Spectroscopy
summary: Crystal engineering offers a route to functional molecular solids through controlled noncovalent interactions. In centrosymmetric crystals, piezoelectricity can be induced by stereoselective doping, where chiral additives are incorporated in a biased orientation that lowers inversion symmetry and generates net polarization. However, the microscopic origin of this polarization, specifically whether it arises primarily from dipole mismatch between the dopant and the host molecule it replaces, or from dopant-induced lattice distortion, remains generally unclear. Here, we disentangle these two contributions by incorporating four chiral N-acetyl-L-amino acids into the centrosymmetric crystal N-acetyl-DL-valine and examining the resulting materials using piezoelectric measurements, density functional theory (DFT), and low-frequency Raman spectroscopy that reveals concentration-dependent symmetry-breaking phenomena not resolved by conventional X-ray diffraction. We show that in the systems studied, macroscopic piezoelectricity correlates directly with the magnitude and orientation of local lattice distortions, whereas dipole mismatch along the polar axis plays a secondary role. These results establish a direct structure–function relation in doped molecular crystals and provide predictive design principles for engineering electromechanical response in molecular crystals through biased local distortions.

screen.tldr: Dopant-induced symmetry breaking in a molecular crystal is linked to piezoelectricity via DFT and Raman, clarifying how local distortions generate polarization.
screen.transfer_note: Raman-sensitive local distortion analysis could help detect subtle symmetry breaking and disorder in candidate molecular crystal polymorphs.

AI.tldr: The study explains how chiral doping can induce piezoelectricity in a centrosymmetric molecular crystal, showing that local lattice distortion is the main driver of the effect rather than simple dipole mismatch.
AI.motivation: The microscopic origin of doping-induced polarization in centrosymmetric crystals is unclear. The authors aim to determine whether piezoelectricity comes mainly from dopant-host dipole mismatch or from dopant-induced lattice distortion.
AI.method: Four chiral N-acetyl-L-amino acids were incorporated into centrosymmetric N-acetyl-DL-valine crystals. The resulting materials were analyzed using piezoelectric measurements, density functional theory (DFT), and low-frequency Raman spectroscopy to probe symmetry breaking and local structural changes.
AI.result: The measured macroscopic piezoelectric response tracked the magnitude and direction of local lattice distortions. Dipole mismatch along the polar axis contributed, but only secondarily. Low-frequency Raman detected concentration-dependent symmetry breaking that conventional X-ray diffraction did not resolve.
AI.conclusion: Biased local lattice distortion is the dominant mechanism behind stereoselectively doped piezoelectric molecular crystals. This provides a structure–function framework and design principle for engineering electromechanical properties in molecular solids.

title: Transport novelty distance: a distributional metric for evaluating material generative models
summary: Abstract Recent advances in generative machine learning have opened new possibilities for the discovery and design of novel materials. However, as these models become more sophisticated, the need for rigorous and meaningful evaluation metrics has grown. Existing evaluation approaches often fail to capture both the quality and novelty of generated structures, limiting our ability to assess true generative performance. In this paper, we introduce the Transport Novelty Distance (TNovD) to judge generative models used for materials discovery jointly by the quality and novelty of the generated materials. Based on ideas from optimal transport theory, TNovD uses a coupling between the features of the training and generated sets, which is used to penalize quality and memorization independently. The two regimes are defined by thresholding the pairwise distances of trained and generated features. The features are generated from crystal structures using a graph neural network that is trained to distinguish between materials, their augmented counterparts, and differently sized supercells using contrastive learning. We evaluate our proposed metric on typical toy experiments relevant for crystal structure prediction, including memorization, noise injection and lattice deformations. Additionally, we validate the TNovD on the MP20 validation set and the WBM substitution dataset, demonstrating that it is capable of detecting both memorized structures and unrealistic material representations that are outside of the training data distribution. We also benchmark the performance of several popular material generative models. While introduced for materials, our TNovD framework is domain-agnostic and can be adapted for other areas, such as images and molecules.

screen.tldr: Introduces a transport-based metric, TNovD, to jointly measure novelty and quality of generated crystal structures using contrastive GNN features.
screen.transfer_note: Could help benchmark CSP generative models by separating memorization from genuinely novel, physically plausible crystal candidates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Transport Novelty Distance (TNovD), a new evaluation metric for generative materials models that jointly measures sample quality and novelty using optimal transport and learned crystal features.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics for generative materials models often miss an important tradeoff: a model can generate high-quality structures that are merely memorized, or novel structures that are unrealistic. The authors aim to create a metric that separates these two failure modes and provides a more faithful assessment of generative performance.
AI.method: TNovD computes a coupling between feature representations of training and generated crystal structures using optimal transport. It then applies threshold-based regimes on pairwise distances to independently penalize poor quality and memorization. The features are learned by a graph neural network trained with contrastive learning to distinguish crystals from augmented versions and differently sized supercells. The metric is tested on toy tasks such as memorization, noise injection, and lattice deformation, and validated on MP20 and WBM datasets.
AI.result: The proposed metric successfully detects memorized structures and unrealistic out-of-distribution material representations. It also differentiates among several popular material generative models, showing stronger diagnostic capability than existing evaluation approaches in the reported experiments.
AI.conclusion: TNovD provides a domain-agnostic framework for evaluating generative models by jointly accounting for novelty and quality. The approach appears useful for materials discovery and may be transferable to other generative domains such as molecules and images.

title: Quantum-Chemically Informed Representation Learning for Molecular Crystals Property Prediction via Multimodal Graph Neural Networks
summary: Machine-learning based modeling of molecular crystals is limited by representations that encode geometric structure while overlooking the electronic features that often govern solid-state behavior. We introduce a multimodal learning framework that integrates crystal graphs with solid-state Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) informed molecular graphs for enhanced predictions of solid-state properties. Our architecture employs modality-specific graph neural network encoders and a bi-directional gated fusion mechanism to capture complementary information between the two representations. When applied to band-gap prediction in organic molecular crystals, the fused model outperforms geometry-only and molecular-only baselines. Analysis of the learned representations reveals that QTAIM descriptors contribute interpretable signals associated with intermolecular interactions and density redistribution within the crystal, highlighting the value of quantum-informed learning for advancing data-driven solidstate modeling.

screen.tldr: Multimodal GNNs combine crystal graphs with QTAIM-informed molecular graphs to improve band-gap prediction for organic molecular crystals.
screen.transfer_note: Quantum-informed descriptors could enrich surrogate models for crystal ranking by capturing intermolecular interactions beyond geometry alone.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multimodal graph learning framework that combines crystal geometry with QTAIM-based electronic descriptors to improve prediction of solid-state properties, especially band gaps in organic molecular crystals.
AI.motivation: Geometry-only representations often miss electronic information that strongly influences solid-state behavior, so the work aims to incorporate quantum-informed features for more accurate and interpretable modeling.
AI.method: The authors build a multimodal architecture with separate graph neural network encoders for crystal graphs and QTAIM-informed molecular graphs, then use a bi-directional gated fusion module to combine the two modalities for property prediction.
AI.result: For band-gap prediction, the fused model outperforms both geometry-only and molecular-only baselines. The learned embeddings also indicate that QTAIM descriptors capture meaningful signals related to intermolecular interactions and density redistribution.
AI.conclusion: Integrating electronic structure information with geometric crystal representations improves both predictive performance and interpretability, showing that quantum-informed multimodal learning is promising for solid-state materials modeling.

title: Hansen Solubility Parameters in Pharmaceutical Cocrystal Screening: From Group Contribution Methods to Machine Learning-Assisted Prediction
comment: World journal of pharmacy and biotechnology.
summary: This review summarizes the theoretical basis of HSPs and discusses the major group contribution methods used for HSP estimation, including the Fedors, Hoy, and Van Krevelen approaches. The application of HSPs in pharmaceutical cocrystal screening, acceptance criteria for cocrystal prediction, and representative case studies involving poorly soluble drugs are critically examined. The advantages and limitations of HSP-based prediction methods are also discussed, highlighting the need for experimental validation of predicted cocrystal systems. Furthermore, recent advances involving machine learning, artificial intelligence, molecular descriptors, and COSMO-RS-assisted screening strategies are reviewed as emerging approaches to improve prediction accuracy and coformer selection. The integration of traditional group contribution methods with modern computational technologies is expected to accelerate pharmaceutical cocrystal discovery and reduce experimental workload. Overall, HSP-based screening remains a valuable and practical tool for early-stage cocrystal development and continues to evolve through advances in data-driven and computational methodologies.
raw_categories: World journal of pharmacy and biotechnology.

AI.motivation: Cocrystal discovery is experimentally expensive and time-consuming, especially for poorly soluble drugs. The review aims to show how HSP-based methods can reduce screening effort while clarifying their strengths, limitations, and need for validation.
AI.method: The paper reviews the theoretical basis of HSPs and summarizes key group contribution estimation methods, including Fedors, Hoy, and Van Krevelen. It also surveys cocrystal screening applications, acceptance criteria, representative case studies, and emerging approaches such as machine learning, molecular descriptors, and COSMO-RS-assisted screening.

Modern computational and AI-assisted strategies are reported as promising ways to improve coformer selection and prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: HSP-based screening remains a useful and accessible tool for pharmaceutical cocrystal development. Its future value will likely come from combining classical group contribution models with machine learning and other computational methods to achieve faster and more accurate discovery.

title: Programming Rotational Register to Prescribe Crystal Polymorphism
summary: Crystal polymorphism underlies many of the distinct properties of condensed matter, yet for atoms and molecules, polymorphs are typically selected by thermodynamics and kinetics rather than by design. Programming crystal polymorphism is particularly challenging for structures that share identical bond connectivity but differ only in the relative orientation of neighboring building blocks. Although programmable self-assembly can prescribe which building blocks bind, it does not directly encode how they are oriented once bonded. Here, we introduce the rotational register, the relative torsional orientation between bonded building blocks, as an independent bond descriptor that complements programmable valence and connectivity. Progressive symmetry breaking of the sequence-programmed DNA pattern at the vertices of DNA tetrahedra provides increasingly precise control over the rotational register, enabling the selective assembly of tetrahedrally coordinated crystal polymorphs: type-II clathrate, cubic diamond, and hexagonal diamond. Cubic and hexagonal diamond differ only in the rotational register encoded at a single vertex type, yet this local rule controls polymorphism while preserving identical bond connectivity. The programmed polymorphs are validated by small-angle X-ray scattering, electron tomography, 2 and both Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, reprogramming the rotational register enables reversible transformation between cubic and hexagonal diamond. These results establish rotational register as a programmable bond descriptor, complementing programmable connectivity with explicit control over the orientation of bonded building blocks.

screen.tldr: DNA tetrahedra are programmed with rotational register to selectively assemble distinct crystal polymorphs, including cubic and hexagonal diamond, via local orientation control.
screen.transfer_note: Local orientational descriptors could inspire symmetry-aware constraints for generating and ranking polymorphs with identical connectivity but different torsional arrangements.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "rotational register" as a new programmable bond descriptor that controls the relative orientation of bonded building blocks, enabling selective assembly of crystal polymorphs with identical connectivity but different orientations.
AI.motivation: Crystal polymorphism is difficult to design because conventional self-assembly mainly controls which components bind, not how they are oriented after binding. The work aims to add explicit orientational control to programmable assembly.
AI.method: The authors use sequence-programmed DNA tetrahedra and progressively break symmetry at their vertices to tune rotational register with increasing precision. This allows selective assembly of tetrahedrally coordinated polymorphs, which are characterized using small-angle X-ray scattering, electron tomography, and Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.result: They successfully programmed assembly of type-II clathrate, cubic diamond, and hexagonal diamond. Cubic and hexagonal diamond were shown to differ by the rotational register at a single vertex type while keeping the same bond connectivity. They also demonstrated reversible transformation between cubic and hexagonal diamond by reprogramming the rotational register.
AI.conclusion: Rotational register functions as a programmable bond descriptor that complements valence and connectivity, providing direct control over bond orientation and enabling rational design and reversible switching of crystal polymorphs.

title: Complex crystal structure prediction using ML-enhanced multi-minima iterative genetic algorithm
summary: Current machine learning (ML) approaches for materials discovery rely heavily on known structural databases, limiting their ability to identify entirely novel structure types. In this work, we develop a multi-minima iterative genetic algorithm (MMIGA) that integrates an artificial-neural-network machine learning (ANN-ML) interatomic potential with an iterative, metadynamics-inspired penalty scheme. We demonstrate the robustness of this method on a complex ternary La-Co-Pb system, characterized by Co-Pb immiscibility and an intricate energy landscape. The ML-enhanced MMIGA successfully predicts the ground-state Pbam structure of the recently synthesized La4Co4Pb antagonistic-pair-phase, a novel structure missed by previous database-reliant ML predictions, while also identifying multiple metastable competing phases. Additionally, we challenged the MMIGA method to predict the structure of La5CoPb2 antagonistic-pair-phase, a new compound discovered during earlier attempts to synthesize the predicted phase La3CoPb. With only knowledge of the composition, our MMIGA approach successfully predicts the orthorhombic structure of La5CoPb2, producing an exact match with the structure independently determined by x-ray diffraction. By efficiently mapping both global minimum and relevant competing metastable states, this approach provides critical theoretical insights into phase selection for novel quantum and magnetic materials.

screen.tldr: ML-enhanced genetic algorithm predicts ground-state and metastable crystal structures for complex ternary compounds, including an experimentally confirmed new phase.
screen.transfer_note: Iterative GA search with ML interatomic potentials and penalty schemes could accelerate polymorph landscape exploration and metastable-state mapping in CSP.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multi-minima iterative genetic algorithm (MMIGA) combined with an ANN-based interatomic potential to discover unknown crystal structures beyond the limits of database-driven ML methods.
AI.motivation: Conventional materials-discovery ML methods depend on known structural databases, which makes them weak at finding truly novel structure types. The goal here is to improve unbiased structure prediction for complex materials with rugged energy landscapes.
AI.method: The authors combine an artificial-neural-network machine-learning interatomic potential with an iterative, metadynamics-inspired penalty scheme inside a multi-minima iterative genetic algorithm. This setup is used to search the energy landscape more broadly and avoid repeatedly converging to already found minima.
AI.result: On the ternary La-Co-Pb system, the method correctly predicts the ground-state Pbam structure of La4Co4Pb and identifies several metastable competing phases. It also predicts the orthorhombic structure of La5CoPb2 from composition alone, matching the structure later confirmed by x-ray diffraction.
AI.conclusion: MMIGA can efficiently discover both global minima and relevant metastable structures without relying on prior structural databases, making it a promising tool for predicting novel phases in complex quantum and magnetic materials.

title: Rapidly Diversifying Hydrogen‐Bonded Organic Frameworks With Permanent Porosity
summary: ABSTRACT Throughout the long history of porous molecular crystals (PMCs), hydrogen‐bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) have experienced a renaissance and have advanced significantly over the past two decades. HOFs can yield large single crystals with fewer defects due to their reversible bonding and dissociation processes, enabling precise analysis of the structure‐property relationship. They are also attracting attention as candidates for sustainable materials. This article reviews the evolution of HOFs (primarily those with permanent porosity) over the past 15 years, based on the molecular structures of their constituent molecules (tectons). HOFs have been synthesized from a wide variety of tectons, ranging from simple substituted benzene derivatives to those with various π‐conjugated polycyclic aromatic cores, as well as with rigid or flexible macrocyclic cores. Subsequently, we would like to focus on several distinctive aspects and concepts of HOFs. These include permanent porosity of rigid HOFs and flexible HOFs, which is crucial for porous materials; isostructural (isoreticular) HOFs, which can provide a series of continuous HOF libraries; and non‐stoichiometrically mixed multicomponent HOFs, which aim to tune functions and create new ones by using multiple types of constituent molecules.

screen.tldr: Review of hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks with permanent porosity, emphasizing tecton design, isostructural series, and multicomponent porous molecular crystals.
screen.transfer_note: Design principles for tectons, isostructural families, and multicomponent assembly could inform candidate generation and ranking in porous molecular crystal searches.

AI.tldr: The abstract reviews the recent progress of hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (HOFs), emphasizing their permanent porosity, structural diversity, and design strategies for tuning properties through rigid, flexible, isostructural, and multicomponent systems.
AI.motivation: The work is motivated by the renewed interest in porous molecular crystals as sustainable materials and by the need to understand how molecular structure controls porosity, crystallinity, and function in HOFs.
AI.method: This is a review article that surveys HOF development over the past 15 years, organizing the literature by tecton type and by key concepts such as permanent porosity, isostructural series, and non-stoichiometric multicomponent frameworks.

title: Turning 3D Molecular Crystals into 2D MoireSuperlattices with Properties Born Out of Bonding at the AngularlyStacked Interfaces
summary: Angular stacking of two-dimensional (2D) nanoscale crystalline sheets into interacting superstructures, such as moiré superlattices, gives rise to potent quantum materials with unusual and remarkable properties. These superlattices are fabricated twist-stacked using mechanical positioning of the constituent lattices; however, their scalable fabrication is challenging. Chemistry-based methods in the liquid media may be helpful in this regard. Here, we report a generalized method for synthesizing multilayered moiré superlattices from covalent molecular crystals, ionic crystals, and metal complex crystals at moderate temperatures in the presence of ultrasonic waves with suitable solvent systems. We also report on the novel optical properties of specific superlattices, arising out of the angularly stacked interfaces. Furthermore, the observation of multilayered moiré superlattices of NaCl and KCl brings in a new perspective in the formation and stability of their 2D hexagonal lattices in such a superstructure. This discovery opens up new options for designing and fabricating moiré superlattices from various molecular materials and for studying their chemistry at the nanoscale.

title: Interface‐Directed High Fluorescence Efficiency Two‐Dimensional Molecular Crystals With Surface‐Exposed Active Sites
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) molecular crystals offer significant advantages for many applications due to their ultrahigh surface-to-volume ratio. Nonetheless, controlling the oriented growth of 2D crystals to expose more active sites remains a challenge. Herein, we develop a strategy that combines molecular design with interfacial assembly to achieve the oriented formation of 2D crystals of Me-FBSe. Uniquely, this architecture preserves the high photoluminescence quantum yield intrinsic to the crystalline state, while simultaneously ensuring the high-density surface exposure of active sites. The integration of high luminescence efficiency and accessible active sites enables ultrasensitive detection of dimethyl sulfide (DMS) vapor at 50 ppb. Notably, this sensing material can detect DMS in aqueous environments via headspace vapor analysis, with a minimum detectable concentration of 100 ppb, demonstrating its reliability in practical monitoring applications. This work establishes a new strategy for the directional exposure of functional groups in high-performance sensors.

AI.method: The authors combine molecular design with interfacial assembly to direct the formation of oriented 2D Me-FBSe crystals, aiming to preserve the intrinsic crystalline photoluminescence quantum yield while maximizing surface-accessible active sites.
